title: Sparse Matrices
definition: A sparse matrix is a matrix in which most of the elements are zero. Storing such matrices using a standard 2D array wastes memory. Sparse matrix representation stores only the non-zero elements.
conceptExplanation: In a sparse matrix, most elements are zero. Instead of storing all m×n elements, we store only the non-zero elements along with their row and column indices. Common representations include: 1) Triplet representation (3 arrays: row, column, value), 2) Linked list representation, 3) Hash mapping.
keyPoints: - Most elements are zero - Special storage needed - Three triplet representation - Linked list representation - Hash mapping
importantTerminology: Sparse matrix, Dense matrix, Triplet representation, Row, Column, Value, Non-zero element
workingPrinciple: The triplet representation stores only non-zero elements as (row, column, value) tuples. For an m×n matrix with s non-zero elements, we store s triplets instead of m×n elements. Linked list representation uses a node structure with row, column, value, and next pointer.
realLifeExample: Scientific computing, matrices in machine learning, graph adjacency matrices, network analysis
dsaExample: Adding two sparse matrices, transposing a sparse matrix, storing a large matrix with few non-zero values efficiently
algorithm:
Sparse Matrix Addition:
1. Read triplets of both matrices
2. Compare row and column indices
3. If same, add values and store result
4. If different, store the smaller index first
5. Continue until all triplets processed
6. Output resultant triplet array
pseudocode:
BEGIN
  READ s1, s2 (number of non-zero elements)
  i = 1; j = 1; k = 1
  WHILE i <= s1 AND j <= s2
    IF A[i].row < B[j].row
      C[k] = A[i]; i = i + 1
    ELSE IF A[i].row > B[j].row
      C[k] = B[j]; j = j + 1
    ELSE
      IF A[i].col < B[j].col
        C[k] = A[i]; i = i + 1
      ELSE IF A[i].col > B[j].col
        C[k] = B[j]; j = j + 1
      ELSE
        C[k].value = A[i].value + B[j].value
        C[k] = A[i]; i = i + 1; j = j + 1
      END IF
    END IF
    k = k + 1
  END WHILE
  // Copy remaining elements\n  WHILE i <= s1
    C[k] = A[i]; i = i + 1; k = k + 1
  END WHILE
  WHILE j <= s2
    C[k] = B[j]; j = j + 1; k = k + 1
  END WHILE
  PRINT C
END
complexity:
Time: Addition O(s1 + s2) where s1, s2 are non-zero elements\nSpace: O(s) for storing s non-zero elements
Compared to O(m×n) for standard representation
applications: Scientific computing, finite element method, graph algorithms, machine learning sparse data
advantages: Memory efficient for matrices with few non-zero elements\nFaster operations on sparse data\nReduces storage from m×n to s (where s << m×n)
limitations: Overhead for matrices that are not sparse\nComplexity in accessing specific elements\nNot suitable for dense matrix operations
commonMistakes: Forgetting to handle remaining triplets after main loop\nIncorrect index comparison in addition\nNot maintaining sorted order of triplets

fiveMarkQuestions.question: Explain sparse matrix representation and addition algorithm.
fiveMarkQuestions.answer: A sparse matrix has most elements as zero. Instead of storing all m×n elements, we store only non-zero elements. Triplet representation uses three arrays/rows: row[], col[], value[] for s non-zero elements. Addition algorithm compares row and column indices of two matrices' triplets: if rows differ, smaller row goes first; if same row, compare columns; if same position, add values. Remaining triplets are copied directly. Result maintains sorted order. This reduces storage from m×n to O(s) where s is number of non-zero elements.

tenMarkQuestions.question: Explain sparse matrix representations and operations in detail.
tenMarkQuestions.answer:
Sparse matrix storage techniques:

1. Triplet Representation: Stores (row, column, value) for each non-zero element in sorted order. Simple but requires sorting.

2. Linked List Representation: Each node contains row, column, value, and next pointer. Allows dynamic operations.

3. Hash Mapping: Uses (row, col) as key and value as data. Provides O(1) access.

Operations:
- Addition: Compare triplets row/column-wise, add values at same positions, maintain sorted order. Complexity: O(s1 + s2).
- Transpose: Convert A[m][n] to A[n][m] by swapping row and column indices. Can be done in O(s) using auxiliary array.
- Fast Transpose: More efficient O(m+n+s) algorithm using row pointer technique.

Applications: Solving large systems where matrices are sparse (scientific computing, FEM), graph adjacency matrices, machine learning (sparse features).

Comparison: Triplet is simple, linked list allows dynamic operations, hash mapping provides fast access.
